Empirical Research Plan – Trade Liberalization and Labor-Market Adjustment in Brazil  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension and a continuous treatment intensity (“dose–response” DID).

Why it fits  
• The 1990–94 tariff cuts created a sharp, policy-driven change that differs in magnitude across 4-digit manufacturing industries.  
• Pre- and post-period data exist for the same firms/industries ➜ panel DID feasible.  
• Because every industry is exposed to the macro shock, cross-sectional differences in the size of the tariff drop provide the counterfactual.  
• The event-study (interacting treatment intensity with year dummies) lets us test parallel trends and trace dynamics (short- vs. long-run).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
TARIFF_DROP_i ≡ (Tariff_i,1989 – Tariff_i,1995) / Tariff_i,1989.  
Interpretation: % reduction in the statutory MFN tariff for industry i.

Binary treatment version for some tables: HIGH_EXPOSURE_i = 1[ TARIFF_DROP_i ≥ median ].

Control group  
Industries (or firms tied to industries) with smaller tariff drops serve as the control (i.e., low-exposure industries).

Timing  
Policy announced 1990, phased in 1991–1993. We code POST_t = 1 for 1991 onward; t = 1990 or 1989 and earlier are pre-treatment.

Unit of analysis  
Primary: firm-year observations, assigned their 4-digit industry’s TARIFF_DROP_i.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of liberalization, high- and low-exposure industries would have followed the same employment/wage paths.  
Plausibility: Reasonable—tariffs were set for political, not recent-trend, reasons. Testable with pre-period event-study coefficients.

A2. Exogeneity of tariff changes: The magnitude of 1990s tariff cuts is orthogonal to contemporaneous labor-market shocks.  
Plausibility: High. Tariff schedule largely harmonized toward a flat structure; cuts were bigger where pre-1990 tariffs were high—reflecting historic protection, not 1980s employment changes.

A3. Stable composition / SUTVA: No large spillovers across industries that contaminate control units, and firm exit/entry does not mechanically depend on tariff drop in a way that biases estimates.  
Plausibility: Some concern (input–output linkages, selection). We will test and, when necessary, instrument for survivorship.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential pre-trends  
• Mitigation: Plot event-study coefficients for −5…−1 years. Include industry-specific linear trends in robustness checks.  

T2. Simultaneous macro reforms (privatization, stabilization plans)  
• Mitigation: Control for industry-year shocks such as state-owned share, index of price stabilization exposure; add region-by-year fixed effects when using firm location.  

T3. Composition bias from firm entry/exit  
• Mitigation: (i) Estimate on balanced panel of continuing firms. (ii) Re-weight by inverse‐probability of survival. (iii) Show that exit probability itself rises with tariff drop but results on incumbent employment remain similar.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # high-dim panel estimators
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load and merge data ------------------------------------------
firms   <- fread("firm_panel_brazil.csv")        # firm-year level outcomes
tariffs <- fread("industry_tariffs_1989_1995.csv") # industry-year tariffs

# Keep baseline and post years we need
tariffs[, tariff_drop := (tariff_1989 - tariff_1995)/tariff_1989]
firms   <- merge(firms, tariffs[, .(industry4, tariff_drop)],
                 by = "industry4", all.x = TRUE)

# 2. Variable construction ----------------------------------------
firms[, post := (year >= 1991)]
firms[, high_exposure := as.integer(tariff_drop >= median(tariff_drop, na.rm=TRUE))]

# Outcomes
firms[, ln_emp   := log(1 + employment)]
firms[, ln_wage  := log(real_avg_wage)]

# 3. Main DID specification ---------------------------------------
# continuous treatment
did_main <- feols(ln_emp ~ post * tariff_drop | firm_id + year,
                  data = firms, cluster = ~industry4)
summary(did_main)

# 4. Event-study (dynamic) ----------------------------------------
esc <- feols(ln_emp ~ i(year, tariff_drop, ref = 1990) | firm_id + year,
             data = firms, cluster = ~industry4)
iplot(esc, main = "Event study: Employment vs. Tariff Drop")

# 5. Robustness: binary treatment, industry-specific trends -------
did_balanced <- feols(ln_emp ~ post * high_exposure | firm_id +
                      year[industry4] + industry4, # industry trends
                      data = firms, cluster = ~industry4)
summary(did_balanced)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory (Heckscher-Ohlin, specific-factors) predicts import-competing industries shrink.  
Prior: A 10-percentage-point larger tariff cut will lower industry employment by ≈5 % in the short run (first 3 years) and wages by ≈2 %. Over 6–8 years the employment gap may narrow to −2 %, wages remain −1 %. Gains may accrue in export-oriented industries but those are our “low-exposure” controls.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
C1 Parallel pre-trends demonstrated: 1  
C2 No anticipation/clean break in treatment: 0.8  
C3 No concurrent shocks differentially correlated: 0.7  
C4 Stable composition / SUTVA: 0.6  
C5 Correct inference (clustering, placebo checks): 1  
Overall average ≈ 0.82 – credible but not bullet-proof.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan delivers transparent, testable causal estimates of Brazil’s early-1990s trade liberalization on employment and wages, distinguishing short-term disruption from longer-term adjustment.
